_readme: Every entry here must be traceable to an official/agricultural-extension source. Do not let any LLM edit this file. Update 'last_verified' whenever you check a source is still live. Dosage/product names are deliberately omitted for MVP — always tell farmers to confirm exact product & dose with local Krishi Vibhag / KVK / a licensed dealer.

Tomato___healthy.symptoms: No visible disease symptoms. Leaves are uniformly green, no spots, wilting, or discoloration.
immediate_actions: No treatment needed.
Continue regular monitoring, ideally twice a week.
prevention: Maintain proper spacing for airflow.
Water at the base, avoid wetting foliage.
Rotate crops each season; avoid planting tomato/potato in the same spot repeatedly.
Tomato___healthy.warning: Re-check the plant if any spots, curling, or yellowing appear later.
Tomato___healthy.source: General good agricultural practice — verify locally with your Krishi Vibhag / nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK).

Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark concentric-ring ('target') spots on older/lower leaves first, yellowing around spots, can spread upward and defoliate the plant if unmanaged.
immediate_actions: Remove and destroy visibly infected lower leaves to slow spread.
Improve airflow around plants; avoid overhead watering.
If disease is spreading, consult your local Krishi Vibhag / KVK / registered pesticide dealer for an approved fungicide and correct dose for your area — do not self-prescribe.
prevention: Use disease-free seed/transplants.
Practice crop rotation (avoid tomato/potato in the same field 2-3 seasons running).
Remove and destroy old crop debris after harvest.
Irrigate so foliage dries quickly (drip preferred over overhead sprinklers).
Tomato___Early_blight.warning: Uncontrolled early blight can significantly reduce marketable yield. Confirm diagnosis with an agricultural officer before spending on treatment, especially if this is your main livelihood crop.
Tomato___Early_blight.source: UC Statewide IPM Program, Early Blight/Tomato (ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/tomato/early-blight/); UConn/UMass Extension early blight management notes.

Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems that enlarge quickly; white fungal growth on leaf undersides in humid/cool weather; dark greasy lesions on fruit. Can defoliate a plant within ~2 weeks in favorable weather.
immediate_actions: This disease spreads very fast in cool, wet weather — act quickly.
Remove and destroy (do not compost) severely infected plants/leaves to reduce spread to neighboring plants.
Avoid overhead irrigation immediately.
Contact your local Krishi Vibhag / KVK urgently — late blight often needs prompt, correctly-timed fungicide application; get local, verified guidance rather than delaying.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seedlings.
Avoid sprinkler irrigation; keep foliage dry.
Remove volunteer tomato/potato plants and nightshade weeds nearby.
Check transplants for symptoms before planting.
Tomato___Late_blight.warning: Late blight is one of the most destructive tomato diseases and can cause severe crop loss very quickly. Treat this as urgent — do not wait to see if it 'goes away'.
Tomato___Late_blight.source: UC Statewide IPM Program, Late Blight/Tomato (ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/tomato/late-blight/); Cornell Vegetables Late Blight guide (vegetables.cornell.edu/crops/tomatoes/late-blight/).

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green/yellow spots on upper leaf surface, with olive-green to grayish-purple fuzzy mold on the underside directly below. Common in humid conditions, especially in polyhouses/greenhouses.
immediate_actions: Increase ventilation and reduce humidity around plants (this disease thrives above ~85% humidity).
Remove and destroy the most affected leaves.
Avoid overhead watering; water at soil level.
If in a polyhouse/greenhouse, widen plant spacing and increase airflow.
prevention: Use resistant varieties where available.
Keep humidity down, especially in protected cultivation.
Avoid overcrowding plants.
Practice crop rotation and remove crop debris after harvest.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.warning: Mainly a greenhouse/polyhouse problem in most regions but can occur in humid open-field conditions too. Confirm with local extension staff if unsure, since it can resemble other leaf-spot diseases.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.source: General extension plant-pathology guidance (Cornell/Clemson HGIC tomato disease fact sheets) — cross-check locally with your KVK for region-specific advice.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark borders and light gray/tan centers, usually starting on lower leaves. Tiny black specks (fungal fruiting bodies) may be visible in the center of spots. Can cause heavy leaf drop if unmanaged.
immediate_actions: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves promptly.
Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet, to reduce spread.
Improve airflow between plants.
Consult your local Krishi Vibhag/KVK if spread continues, for a locally approved fungicide and correct dose.
prevention: Rotate crops away from tomato/potato family for at least 2 seasons.
Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest — the fungus survives on old plant material.
Mulch around plants to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.warning: Can be confused with early blight — Septoria spots are smaller and lack the 'target-ring' pattern. Get a second opinion if treatment doesn't help within a week or two.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.source: General plant-pathology extension guidance (Cornell/Clemson/UMass tomato disease fact sheets) — verify locally with your KVK.

Tomato___Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider.disease: Two-Spotted Spider Mite infestation (pest, not a disease)
Tomato___Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow/white stippling (tiny dots) on leaves, leaves may turn bronze/yellow and dry out, fine webbing visible on the underside of leaves or between leaves in heavy infestations. Worse in hot, dry weather.
immediate_actions: Spray plants (especially leaf undersides) with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites — often enough for mild infestations.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which favors mite population growth.
For heavier infestations, consult your local Krishi Vibhag/KVK about an approved miticide — spider mites resist many general pesticides, so a targeted product is important.
prevention: Keep plants adequately watered — drought-stressed plants are more susceptible.
Encourage natural predators (e.g. predatory mites, ladybird beetles) by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum spraying.
Monitor regularly during hot, dry spells.
Tomato___Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider.warning: This is a pest infestation, not a fungal/viral disease — treatment approach is different from the other categories here.
Tomato___Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider.source: General IPM extension guidance on two-spotted spider mite in tomato — verify locally with your KVK for region-appropriate miticides.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mottled light/dark green mosaic pattern on leaves, leaf curling/distortion, stunted plant growth, sometimes malformed or discolored fruit.
immediate_actions: There is no chemical cure for viral infection — focus is on containment.
Remove and destroy infected plants to prevent spread to healthy plants.
Wash hands and disinfect tools (e.g. with a dilute bleach or soap solution) after handling infected plants, since the virus spreads easily by contact.
Avoid working with tobacco products before handling plants — ToMV can spread via tobacco mosaic virus-contaminated hands.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties where available.
Disinfect tools and hands between plants, especially when pruning/staking.
Control weeds that can host the virus.
Avoid reusing infected plant debris or seed saved from infected plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.warning: Infected plants cannot be cured — the goal is stopping spread to protect the rest of the field. Confirm diagnosis with a local expert since symptoms can overlap with other viruses (e.g. mosaic caused by ToMV vs TMV vs other viral complexes).
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.source: General plant virology extension guidance — verify locally with your KVK / State Agriculture University (e.g. Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth, Rahuri, for Maharashtra).
